faqs.answer: Dots is a persistent agent on OpenAI's cloud: it learns your preferences and keeps working between chats. GAIA is the open alternative with memory, 50+ tools, and self-hosting.
faqs.question: How is GAIA different from OpenAI Dots?

faqs.answer: GAIA offers a free tier, and Pro is a flat ${{PRO_MONTHLY_PRICE}}/month. Self-hosted GAIA has no per-task metering at all.
faqs.question: How much does GAIA cost?

faqs.answer: Start with Gmail and Calendar for context, then add Slack or your task tool. GAIA's memory starts building from the first connected day.
faqs.question: How do I switch to GAIA?

gaiaAdvantages: Persistent memory that compounds across every task
50+ integrations with email, calendar, tasks, and chat
Fully open source and self-hostable via Docker
Works in WhatsApp and Telegram, not one chat surface
gaiaReplaces: Always-on tasks you want running on infrastructure you control
Work that spans email plus calendar plus tasks
Follow-ups that need doing, not just answering
Automations you rebuild every time from scratch
metaDescription: Want Dots-style help in the open? GAIA is an open-source OpenAI Dots alternative with memory, 50+ tools, and self-hosting.
metaTitle: Best OpenAI Dots Alternative: Full AI OS
migrationSteps: List the Dots tasks you want running on infrastructure you control
Connect Gmail and Calendar to give GAIA your working context
Rebuild your most repeated Dots request as a GAIA workflow
Let GAIA run it proactively instead of prompting each time
name: OpenAI Dots
painPoints: Persistent memory that lives inside OpenAI's closed cloud, not under your control
Locked to ChatGPT, Slack, and Teams surfaces, with texting still to come
Your agent runs on OpenAI's servers, so your context stays on their infrastructure
Closed and still evolving, so capabilities shift under you
No open code and no self-hosted option for private or regulated work
tagline: Persistent help that stays in OpenAI's cloud.
whyPeopleLook: Dots proves always-on help is useful. Users look for an alternative when they want the same persistence with open code: an assistant that remembers, connects to tools, and runs on infrastructure they control.
